name: Aristotle
role: Greek philosopher (384-322 BC), author of the Politics and Nicomachean Ethics
summary: Aristotle held that the city exists by nature for the good life and that rule should follow virtue and law rather than force. He defended natural slavery, male authority in the household, private ownership with common use, and a mixed polity resting on a large middle class. He condemned usury and tyranny and wanted education to be public and common.

property-fundamental.rationale: Politics II.5 defends private ownership against Plato's communal property, but he also has the legislator regulate it (II.7, VI.4) and makes use common; he gives no 'right hard to override' position.

cut-welfare.rationale: Politics VI.5 says democratic demagogues who share out surplus revenue are 'pouring water into a sieve' and prefers one lump grant to buy land or tools; he does not claim welfare creates dependency, so evidence points both ways.

state-harmful.rationale: Politics I.2: the city exists by nature and precedes the individual; man is by nature a political animal, and he without it is a beast or a god.

traditional-family.rationale: Politics I.2 makes the household the first natural community from which the city grows, and II.3-5 criticises Plato's community of wives and children as weakening affection and care.

gradual-change.rationale: Politics II.8 says laws may be changed as arts advance, but making it easy to abolish laws weakens them, since law 'derives all its strength from custom', so small faults are better left.

experts-over-public.rationale: Politics III.11 says the many together may judge better than experts and should elect and audit officials, but 'it is not safe' to give them the highest offices.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Politics VI.4 recommends caps on how much land one may hold and a democracy of husbandmen, VI.5 would help the poor buy 'a little field', and IV.11 prefers a large middle rank of moderate means.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Politics III.14-17 sets out kinds of kingship and says it fits a people with a family of surpassing virtue; NE VIII.10 calls monarchy the best form; hereditary succession draws doubts (III.15).

democracy-best.rationale: NE VIII.10 ranks monarchy best and democracy the 'least vicious' of the deviant forms; Politics III.7 calls democracy a deviation, though IV and VI give it a place.

natural-rulers.rationale: Politics I.4-6: some people are slaves by nature, fit only to be governed, and some are marked from birth to rule; the soul rules the body, the male the female, the free man the slave. Book III adds that a man of supreme virtue should be perpetual king (III.13).

war-builds-character.rationale: Politics VII.15 says war makes men just and temperate while peace breeds insolence, but VII.14 criticises Sparta for training for war alone; evidence points both ways.

separate-church-state.rationale: Politics VII.8-10 makes a priesthood one of the city's offices, held by elder citizens, with worship paid from public land; there is no separation.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Politics II.7 argues against Phaleas' equalising property: it is not the legislator's task to equalise circumstances but fix a medium; similarity of sentiment through education matters more than equal wealth.

self-interest-moral.rationale: NE IX.8 asks whether to love oneself best, noting bad men do and the good man acts for honour; Politics II.5 says loving oneself is natural but censured if excessive; evidence is mixed.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Politics VIII.1: no citizen belongs to himself but to the state, each being a part of it whose duty is to regard the good of the whole; the language of rights is absent.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Politics I.8: nature made plants for animals and animals for man, and so 'she has made all these things for men'; this treats nature as valuable for human use.

limit-population.rationale: Politics II.6 says it is more necessary to limit the increase of citizens than to regulate property, and VII.16 sets marriage and childbearing ages in the best city.

conscription.rationale: Politics IV.13 describes fines on the rich for not bearing arms or attending gymnastics, and VII.9 has citizens serve as soldiers while young, then counsellors and priests.

total-state.rationale: Politics VIII.1 and NE X make education and manners a public matter, and VII.17 regulates art, but I.9 and II.5 leave property and household production private; evidence points both ways.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Politics VII.2 and VII.14 reject training citizens to conquer neighbours and say war is for peace; the exception is war on those 'intended by nature for slavery' (I.7).

bound-labor.rationale: Politics VII.9-10: in the best city the land belongs to citizens, worked by slaves or barbarian servants of differing nations, 'if one had one's choice'; no explicit legal tie to the land, so low.

universal-morality.rationale: NE V.10 holds that while many just things are conventional, some exist by nature, and one constitution 'by nature would be best in all places'.

single-common-good.rationale: Politics III.7: constitutions that aim at the common good are right, those aiming at the rulers' own are deviant; III.9 says the city exists for living well, not just defence or trade. He still weighs rich and poor claims (III.9, IV.9).

school-vouchers.rationale: Politics VIII.1: education should be 'one and the same' for all and a common public care, 'not the individual's', as when each parent teaches as he pleases.

rule-by-example.rationale: NE X says the mass obey compulsion and punishment rather than reason, so laws with compulsory force are needed, and Politics III.16 prefers law to rulers; the example of rulers is not the main tool.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Politics I.13 says courage in a man is commanding, in a woman obeying, 'silence is a woman's ornament'; II.9 faults Sparta for letting women govern and holds women's liberties hurtful to the city.

ban-interest.rationale: Politics I.10: usury is 'most reasonably detested' as money bred of money, the form of money-making 'most against nature'; VI.4 cites approvingly an old law forbidding adding to one's patrimony by usury.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Politics III.7: states ruling for the common good are right, those serving the rulers' own interest are deviant; so he sees class rule as a corruption, not the essence of the state.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Politics III.9: the city was not founded merely to preserve life, property or to prevent mutual injury or trade; it exists for living well and its lawgiver must attend to citizens' virtue and vice.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Politics I.5-6 and I.13 hold that natural slaves lack the deliberative faculty and a woman's is without authority, so he denies equal standing; in Book III citizens share offices by merit, not equally by birth.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Politics V.10 says kingship is 'voluntarily submitted to' while tyranny is not, but I.5 justifies rule over natural slaves without consent; the legitimacy test is the common good.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Politics IV.15 and VI.5 describe lot as a democratic mode and election as aristocratic, and recommend mixing both for magistrates; he does not argue for lot alone.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Politics VII.17 has magistrates ensure there are no obscene statues or pictures, bars the young from iambics and comedies, and keeps children from whatever is loose and offensive.

people-in-arms.rationale: Politics IV.13 and VII.9 make the arms-bearing citizens the governing body, with young citizens as soldiers; he does not treat a professional army as the model.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Politics VI.4 calls the democracy of husbandmen the best kind because such citizens are least inclined to idle assembly-going and so let the best persons hold office; Book VII.9 bars mechanic and merchant life in the best city.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Politics VII.7 ranks peoples: northern peoples courageous but unintelligent, Asiatics clever but unspirited and enslaved, Greeks combining both and 'capable of commanding the whole world' if united.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Politics VII.17: magistrates are to forbid obscene pictures and statues, except to certain gods, and obscene talk; this is not framed as an adult prohibition.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Politics III.2 reports the popular rule that a citizen is born of citizen parents but calls it a simple account that breaks down for founders and enrolled foreigners, and defines the citizen by exercising office.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Politics II.5: 'best to have property private, but to make the use of it common', with the legislator to bring this about; SEP notes every citizen of the best city has a just claim to property.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Reviewer: a priesthood held by citizens and funded from public land is nearby evidence; he does not address curbing religious institutions' power or property. No recorded position found.

character-from-environment.rationale: NE II.1: virtues come neither by nature nor against it; we are given the capacity and perfect it by habit and upbringing. He treats natural slavery as innate (Politics I.5), which this ignores.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Politics III.16: 'law is reason without desire' and it is more proper that law govern than any citizen; IV.4 says law should be supreme. III.13 excepts a hypothetical man of superhuman virtue.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Politics IV.11: the middle-rank state, mixing oligarchy and democracy, is best for most cities; IV.9 and V.8 describe blending the rich's and people's claims. His ideal state is aristocratic, not mixed.

land-redistribution.rationale: Politics VI.3 says confiscating the property of the rich by majority vote would be unjust; II.7 criticises levelling schemes; yet VI.5 would give the poor funds to buy small plots, so opposition is to confiscation.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Politics IV.4 condemns a democracy where the people's votes override the laws as like a tyranny, saying law must be supreme and 'decrees cannot be general'.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Politics I.5-7 holds mastery is advantageous to natural slaves and that war against those 'intended by nature for slavery' is by nature just; but he does not describe rule as temporary or as improvement, so only partly matches.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Politics VI.5 says it is worthy of 'a sensible and generous nobility' to support the poor from what is needed and induce them to work, and that the rich should pay for necessary services.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Politics VII.2-3 considers the public and the philosophic lives and holds the active life happiest for a city; NE X.7 calls contemplation the highest happiness. This points both ways.

filial-duty.rationale: Nicomachean Ethics VIII (disowning a parent) says a son can never repay his father and may never disown him; IX.2 says that, for maintenance, we should help our parents in preference to others as their debtors.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Politics VII.1 rebukes those who seek riches, power and honour 'without bounds', saying external goods do not produce virtue; I.9-10 limits natural wealth to what the household needs.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Inferred: NE V.2 says the laws aim at the common good and the lawful is just, and Politics III.15 says free people act only in conformity to the law, so he treats obeying law as a duty; he never states the question.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Politics VII.16 has the legislator regulate marriage by law: the ages of man and woman, season, and the period of childbearing, as a matter of public concern; he never questions marriage as an institution.

socialized-care.rationale: Politics II.3-5 rejects holding wives and children in common and having the city raise children, arguing that care weakens when shared; household management stays with the family (I.12-13).

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Politics VII.8 lists arms among the city's necessities, saying the community needs an armed force within it to support its government and defend against outsiders.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Politics III.15 asks whether the king's family is to reign, noting the children may turn out poorly and that a king is unlikely to bar them, which 'requires greater virtue than is to be met with in human nature'.

property-franchise.rationale: Politics IV.13 supports a census for office in a polity, set low so citizens form the greater part of the people; VII.9 gives full citizenship only to men with leisure and landed property.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Politics IV.4: where decrees rather than laws rule there is 'no free state'; law ought to be supreme and magistrates decide only particular cases; III.16 says law cannot cover every case.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Politics IV.11: a city of the very rich and very poor consists 'of slaves and masters, not freemen', so the middle rank is best for lasting free government.

term-limits.rationale: Politics V.8 recommends the democratic rule that no one hold office longer than six months so all of the same rank have a turn, because long tenure lets magistrates do mischief and tyrannies arise from it; VI.2 says no office should be for life.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Politics I.12: the male is by nature superior to the female and governs the household, though over a wife with constitutional rather than despotic rule; I.13: the woman's deliberative faculty is weak.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Politics III.1 and III.5 treat sojourners and aliens as not sharing in the honours of the state, defining the citizen by share in judicial and civil office.

person-over-state.rationale: Politics VIII.1 says every citizen belongs to the state as a part of it, but III.9 says the state exists for its members' living well; evidence points both ways.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Politics VII.14 says citizens should be fit for war so as not to be enslaved, not to enslave others; I.7 allows war to subject natural slaves, so only partly defensive.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Politics II.9 faults the Spartan law under which about two-fifths of the land was owned by women as heiresses, saying it would be better to allow them none or a little or a regulated amount.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: NE V.15 defends equity as correcting law 'where law is defective by reason of its universality', so judges must have discretion beyond a fixed rule.

women-suffrage.rationale: Politics I.13 says a woman's deliberative power is 'a weak one'; II.9 says women's power in public affairs harmed Sparta; Book III defines the citizen by sharing in judicial and civil office, which women do not hold in his schemes (SEP notes women were excluded).

simple-living.rationale: Politics I.9-10 treats household wealth as limited to what life requires and II.7 says desires should be regulated; this is not a call for self-sufficient austerity, so low.

notes: Chapter numbers follow the Ellis translation of the Politics (Gutenberg #6762, numbered as printed) and the Gutenberg Nicomachean Ethics. The Ellis text elides the sentence on abortion and exposure in Politics VII.16, so abortion and infant exposure are left null. Wikipedia gives birth as 384 BC; the catalog uses 384/383. The Politics text reached by the audit is a translation, not the Greek.
